title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is training a generative AI system on copyrighted recordings without obtaining licenses or paying rights holders. This happened at the data-collection stage, before any model was deployed to users, meaning the legal and rights-clearance problem was embedded in the system from the start. Catching it would have required auditing the training dataset for rights status before training began, a step that was apparently not taken or not taken adequately.

The incident involves multiple overlapping legal disputes: major labels suing over alleged unauthorized use of their catalogs, a class action brought by independent artists that a court declined to dismiss, a musicians' union lawsuit over a subsequent licensing deal, and a second Sony lawsuit covering tens of thousands of additional recordings that a judge initially barred from the original case. Some disputes settled into licensing partnerships while others remain in litigation. The scale alleged, tens of thousands of individual sound recordings, points to systematic rather than incidental use of protected material during training.

What is not established is whether any court has found Udio liable for copyright infringement. The lawsuits are allegations, the settlements resolve claims without admissions, and the ongoing cases have not produced final verdicts.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements that resolve claims the company used copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. UMG had accused Udio of using hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" to create similar melodies without permission or compensation. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream and share their creations. Artists can opt into the platform and will receive compensation, though specific details remain undisclosed.

This settlement marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label and reflects the ongoing tension between AI companies and the entertainment industry. Founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, Udio has attracted millions of users since launching. The company's backers include music artist will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. UMG also announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers, signaling the music industry's evolving approach to embracing AI technology while protecting copyrights.
